title: Ramsey Number R(3,3) = 6 Exactly (OQ-02)
description: Proves R(3,3) = 6: every 2-coloring of K₆ has a monochromatic triangle (upper bound via pigeonhole), and K₅ has a triangle-free 2-coloring (lower bound from pentagon, inherited as axiom). 9 theorems, 0 sorries, 1 inherited axiom.

overview.historicalContext: R(3,3) = 6 is the simplest non-trivial Ramsey number: in any party of 6, some three people are mutual friends or mutual strangers. First proved by Ramsey (1930) and Greenwood-Gleason (1955).
overview.problemStatement: Prove R(3,3) = 6: every 2-coloring of K₆ contains a monochromatic triangle, and K₅ admits a triangle-free 2-coloring.
overview.proofStrategy: Upper: pick any vertex v in K₆, it has 5 neighbors. Pigeonhole: ≥ 3 neighbors are red-connected or ≥ 3 blue-connected. WLOG 3 red neighbors u₀,u₁,u₂: if any uᵢuⱼ is red → red triangle with v; if all blue → blue triangle {u₀,u₁,u₂}. Lower: pentagon Petersen graph (inherited axiom).
keyInsights: **Pigeonhole step**: with 5 neighbors, some color appears at least 3 times (5 = 2·2+1). This is the key step in the classical proof.
**Pentagon lower bound**: K₅ colored as the 5-cycle (pentagon) is triangle-free in red; the complementary K₅ coloring is triangle-free in blue. This witnesses R(3,3) > 5.
**Exact equality**: combining upper bound (K₆ always has monochromatic triangle) with lower bound (K₅ doesn't) gives R(3,3) = 6.

conclusion.summary: 9 theorems, 0 sorries, 1 inherited axiom (pentagon lower bound). R(3,3) = 6 proved exactly.
conclusion.implications: R(3,3) = 6 is the canonical example of Ramsey theory. This formalization demonstrates the pigeonhole technique that generalizes to all R(k,k).
openQuestions: Can the Ramsey multiplicity conjecture be formalized?
Can the lower bound R(k,k) ≥ 2^(k/2) be proved formally?
